It runs chunk-cache and retained immediate-baseline variants through the same move-jump-edit PilotScript, requires identical non-renderer semantic reports and byte-exact screenshots, scans generated C/headers for zero goto statements, allocator calls, and hxrt references, and reports timings, draw/rebuild counts, explicit 196816-byte cache payload (excluding unmeasured ABI padding), generated C/header size, binary size, pinned native/Raylib facts, scene/input hashes, viewport, warmup, and sampling method. The cheap comparison/parity/artifact contract now runs under test:caxecraft-pilot; playable snapshots, terrain Eval/native/sanitizer, gameplay, CI/toolchain policy, and Haxe formatting pass. The command intentionally rejects macOS Memory before compiling because haxe_c-d8f owns the missing clock. It explicitly labels the retained renderer as a generated-Haxe baseline, not the still-required handwritten-C baseline. Remaining before closure: execute and review paired Linux timings and add the fair equivalent handwritten C/raylib comparison (or obtain an explicit scope split).
The full paired benchmark is now wired into both required Linux Raylib-headless GCC/Clang matrix entries. It reuses the job's already checksum-verified Raylib build, keeps the separate sanitizer pilot, uploads both variant reports/screenshots plus the combined comparison, and is guarded by CI-policy snippets. Local CI/toolchain policy and whitespace checks pass; execution timing remains available only when the Linux job runs.

title: Add a typed native TUI frontend to the todo showcase
description:
Context: The canonical E9 todo showcase currently proves a scriptable CLI, SQLite integration, compile-time schema/command generation, and portable domain logic, but it does not prove an interactive native terminal application. A TUI is a strong product demonstration because it combines Haxe ergonomics with ordinary C libraries and native executable behavior.

Scope: Add a second todo frontend over the exact same typed domain, validation, command model, and SQLite repository used by the CLI. Exercise a typed terminal-library binding or target-owned terminal adapter, input events, resize, incremental rendering, Unicode text, resource ownership, errors, and deterministic cleanup. Keep the CLI as the non-interactive baseline and acceptance interface.

Non-scope: A graphical desktop UI, compiler special cases, raw __c__ injection, duplicated business logic, or a claim that every terminal/platform is supported. Split any new compiler/runtime/library capability into its owning bead rather than hiding it in example code.

Product value: The example should make visible why Haxe helps: exhaustive typed UI states, reusable portable domain code, compile-time schema/command derivation, and safer native-library integration while still producing inspectable warning-clean C.
design: Use four explicit layers: portable todo domain; SQLite repository; scriptable CLI adapter; interactive TUI adapter. The CLI and TUI must share application commands and services rather than call each other or fork the domain. Select the terminal backend through the normal bindgen/adapter policy after portability and ABI evidence; do not bake a third-party ABI into handwritten Haxe declarations without probes. CI should drive a deterministic terminal transcript or pseudo-terminal harness rather than relying on timing or screenshots alone.
acceptance_criteria:
- examples/todo-tui has a schema-valid case.json with role example and declared semantic assertions.
- CLI and TUI share the same domain, validation, application commands, migrations, and SQLite repository; no business-logic fork exists.
- The TUI covers list/filter/add/edit/complete/delete/help, terminal resize, empty/error states, and clean shutdown.
- Terminal integration uses typed bindings or a target-owned adapter, contains no raw __c__, and documents ownership, encoding, portability, and runtime effects.
- A deterministic transcript or pseudo-terminal harness runs in CI without depending on wall-clock timing; generated C is warning-clean under required GCC and Clang lanes.
- Runtime-plan, generated-C inspection, sanitizer/resource-cleanup evidence, and supported/unsupported hosted environments are documented honestly.
- The walkthrough explains the Haxe advantage and retains the CLI as a stable automation/accessibility path.

title: [HXC-E9] Examples, todo CLI, documentation, and adoption
description:
Stable plan key: E9
Milestone: M9
Source: docs/specs/beads-plan.json and docs/PRD.md

Outcome: Prove the product through honest, polished examples and a macro-powered SQLite todo CLI.

Scope: Coordinate the acceptance-tested child issues for this milestone. Parent-child hierarchy is structural and does not imply blocking.

Execution: Children may proceed in parallel unless an explicit blocking edge says otherwise.

## Success Criteria

- examples use no unapproved `__c__`;
- todo generated C is reviewed against a hand-written baseline;
- docs state limitations honestly;
- benchmark results are reproducible.

title: Localize Caxecraft conversation speaker display names
description: The conversation panel currently derives a readable uppercase fallback from an authored speaker ID such as guide.nia. Extend reloadable content with an explicit localized speaker display name so creators can name NPCs and narrators without changing compiled Haxe. Keep the fallback for older packs and never add campaign-specific ID mappings to the engine.
acceptance_criteria: Reloadable content can provide an en and es-MX speaker display name; the runtime validates and resolves it with the map locale fallback; old packs retain a readable ID-derived fallback; portraits and dialogue continue to use the same authored speaker identity; tests use synthetic names and the real campaign receives only a light visual review.
notes: Implemented 2026-08-12. CAXEMAP 1 now accepts speaker <npc-object-id> name <text>. The parser retains source location, semantic validation rejects duplicate records and non-NPC targets, the canonical writer sorts records by speaker ID, and message validation checks localized name references. RuntimeLevelPresentation copies and resolves names with the map's default-locale fallback. The HUD uses the authored name and keeps its existing readable ID-derived fallback for old maps. The same speaker ID still selects dialogue and portrait. Added synthetic en/es-MX expectations and negative codec cases. Added Nia, Ceesh, Moss, and Fallskeeper names to reloadable campaign maps. No campaign name mapping entered compiled Haxe. Evidence: scenario-model passed through Haxe and native C; content metadata check passed; a clean isolated compile-only build and native link passed; Adventure journey passed at 1280x720 with two identical semantic runs; visual review showed Nia from map data with her portrait. Runtime-level-loader's name assertions pass before an unrelated deterministic stateful-collision check returns code 122; haxe_c-okdg owns that failure without weakening it.
close_reason: Reloadable localized speaker names, old-pack fallback, shared speaker identity, synthetic checks, and the real visual tracer are complete.

title: Avoid per-draw copies for safe runtime Raylib text
description: Caxecraft now safely copies arbitrary Haxe String views before passing them to Raylib as terminated C text. This fixes a real abort, but dynamic HUD and dialogue drawing can allocate once per call. Design a typed borrow-or-copy adapter that reuses already terminated views and creates owned temporary storage only when required. Preserve CStringRef's zero-copy, fail-closed contract and do not make the runtime borrow operation allocate implicitly.
acceptance_criteria: A reusable typed API accepts any embedded-NUL-free Haxe String view for one non-retaining C call; already terminated views remain allocation-free; interior views receive correctly terminated temporary storage with explicit lifetime; embedded NUL fails before C observes truncation; focused native tests cover both branches and Caxecraft can use the API without campaign-specific code; allocation measurements show the common HUD path no longer copies every draw.

title: Restore the plain Caxecraft build-only lane
description: The documented npm run caxecraft:play -- --build-only command currently stops at the generated-source guard because the selected variant omits RuntimeContentGeneration_loadRuntimeContent(. The adventure live-agent variant still generates, links, and launches correctly. Diagnose variant selection or guard ownership without weakening runtime-content evidence.
acceptance_criteria: The documented plain --build-only command succeeds with the intended runtime-content path, or its documented contract and guard are corrected with focused evidence. Adventure and live-agent variants remain green.

title: Harden live Piloscript for multi-stage campaign play
description: The live agent can play one level in several bounded batches, but the durable graphical journey still fails when an Underworks route crosses into a second runtime-published level. An invalid live batch whose hold exceeded its declared frame count also terminated the host instead of returning a recoverable protocol rejection. Keep this work separate from campaign authoring so content can continue.
acceptance_criteria: A reloadable Piloscript journey can cross at least one campaign transition and verify observations after the second content publication without campaign-specific compiled code. The live JSONL session returns a structured rejection for an invalid batch and remains available for the next valid batch. A focused generic regression covers both behaviors, and one real Underworks-to-Forge route proves them through the native game.
notes: Browser finale play on 2026-08-11 reproduced two live-session gaps. The game continues simulating while the agent waits between batches, so an idle session can take damage or die. Campaign confirmation also became unreliable when selection and launch were split across batches, and one longer valid multi-stage batch exited status 0 before returning a response. The launcher now preserves the real structured protocol error instead of masking it as a missing screenshot. Generic world JSON now reports the nearby hostile actor with authored ID, position, and controller phase; this was necessary to diagnose a boss that crossed a sealed gate. The deterministic reloadable browser-chamber journey remains the current complete proof. Keep this issue open for paused-between-batches semantics, recoverable invalid requests, reliable multi-stage campaign launch/transition, and focused protocol coverage.

title: Render stateful mechanisms as oriented 3D props
description: StatefulObjectRenderer ignores authored yaw for wide textured boxes and draws every small interactive object as a camera-facing billboard. The result is visible in real play: rotated gates can appear edge-on, while switches, relays, winches, glyph controls, and notes look detached from the voxel world and can intersect nearby terrain. Preserve NPC billboards in their separate actor renderer. Render stateful world mechanisms as compact 3D props and apply validated yaw to non-square bounds without recognizing campaign IDs or coordinates.
design: Use the existing stateful-object renderer and content-owned bounds/atlas cell. Large objects remain textured boxes, with width/depth and texture orientation following the admitted quarter-turn yaw. Small stateful objects use one compact textured 3D pedestal assembled from bounded primitives; their atlas cell remains the content-owned identity/state surface. NPC and item rendering stay unchanged. Do not add a model format, campaign-name switch, new asset, or broad presentation schema until real content needs more than this current mechanism family.
acceptance_criteria: A focused renderer projection proves non-square bounds swap at yaw 90/270 and remain unchanged at yaw 0/180; small stateful objects select the 3D mechanism path while large gates select the oriented box path; native C renders a real switch as a grounded 3D prop with no billboard clipping and a rotated gate with visual bounds aligned to collision; existing interaction, object states, atlas lookup, cleanup, NPC billboards, and content-only reload remain unchanged.
notes:
Observed in a real Ashfall frame on 2026-08-11: the root-brace/winch visual is a flat camera-facing sprite against voxel terrain. The repository owner requested 3D switches and other interactive world props while explicitly keeping NPCs 2D for now. The earlier issue contract preserved small billboards; this updated contract supersedes that choice using current visual evidence.
Implementation evidence (2026-08-11):
- Red state: Ashfall's root brace and related small stateful mechanisms used camera-facing atlas billboards. The reviewed game frame showed unrelated atlas fragments and no world-space depth. Large stateful boxes also ignored authored quarter-turn yaw.
- Independent oracle: reloadable content owns bounds, presentation atlas cell, and validated yaw. The generic renderer must use those facts without campaign IDs; the separate actor renderer remains the owner of NPC billboards.
- Green state: small stateful objects now use a grounded 3D pedestal whose body retains the content-owned atlas cell. Large structures use oriented bounds for yaw 0/90/180/270. A live Ashfall agent session interacted with ash.root-brace and showed stable 3D props with no sprite clipping.
- Verification: npm run test:caxecraft-presentation (Eval and native C, sanitizers); exact memory-software adventure executable rebuilt and launched (137 native object cache hits, one renderer miss); npm run test:all-sources; npm run caxecraft:content:check; npm run format:haxe:check; git diff --check.
- Scope: NPCs intentionally remain 2D. This does not add a general model format or campaign-specific rendering.
- Separate finding: the plain --build-only invocation currently trips the runtime-content-loader generated-source guard. The exact adventure/agent variant succeeds; this finding is not counted as renderer evidence.
close_reason: Small stateful controls now render as grounded 3D props, large structures honor quarter-turn yaw, and NPC billboards remain separate. Focused native/sanitizer checks and a live Ashfall interaction confirm the requested visual seam.

title: Let live agent batches use intermediate capture checkpoints
description: In a live agent session, a request with an intermediate capture emits a normal observation before the batch-complete observation. The host reads the first observation as the response and rejects its checkpoint screenshot name as unknown, even though the game remains semantically correct.
design: Make the host and game distinguish checkpoint observations from the one terminal response for a request, or intentionally support an ordered response stream. Preserve bounded timeouts, screenshot confinement, monotonically ordered sequence IDs, and normal non-agent Piloscript captures.
acceptance_criteria: A live batch with one intermediate capture and one final result returns deterministically without an unknown-screenshot error; the intermediate and terminal observations cannot be confused; malformed or missing terminal responses still fail closed; ordinary content-feedback checkpoint screenshots remain unchanged.

title: Prevent distance overflow in live agent observations
description: The live JSON observer squares milli-block deltas in 32-bit Int arithmetic. A mechanism 47 blocks from the player reports a negative distanceSquaredMilliBlocks value, which can misorder or confuse nearby state for an agent playing a larger level.
design: Compute the bounded distance in a representation that cannot overflow for every validated CAXEMAP dimension. Keep the wire field deterministic and preserve generic object selection; do not special-case Underworks or one object ID.
acceptance_criteria: A focused boundary case is red with the current negative value; minimum and maximum legal world deltas produce non-negative correctly ordered observations on Eval and generated native C; a live large-level observation no longer reports a negative distance; existing nearby ordering stays stable.

title: Restore the broad Caxecraft loader build below its focused timeout
description: The runtime-level-loader Haxe-to-C generation exceeded its 60-second bound twice after the physical world doubled to 64x16x32. The focused terrain, resolver, water, and session owners remain fast and green. The broad loader lane passes when its generation stage has a bounded 120-second allowance, so this is workflow cost rather than semantic failure.
design: Measure cold and warm compiler-server phases on an otherwise representative host. Attribute time to typing, lowering, generated runtime planning, or output. Remove redundant work or split only if each resulting lane retains distinct contract evidence. Keep the temporary 120-second case-specific bound until measured evidence supports a lower bound.
acceptance_criteria: Cold and warm runtime-level-loader phase timings are recorded; the first material bottleneck is identified; the lane returns below 60 seconds or receives a reviewed evidence-backed budget; no semantic, native, sanitizer, or generated-structure evidence is dropped.
notes: Connected-region follow-up (2026-08-10): campaign-runtime now parses the shipped compact Evergrove entry and 64-wide Western Falls destination. Its unoptimized native run exceeded the prior 40-second bound twice in isolation. A case-specific 120-second native bound retained the same Eval/native, generated-structure, and sanitizer evidence; the complete lane passed in 185.26 seconds (176.02 user, 3.99 system). The reload-only production-loader check remained 20.96 seconds and the graphical content journey about 35 seconds with no compile or link. Measure and reduce the backstop separately; do not put it in the content-authoring loop.

title: Replace the Caxecraft Python launcher with a Haxe-authored CLI
description: Replace examples/caxecraft/play.py incrementally with a repository-owned Haxe launcher compiled through haxe.c. The current Python file coordinates build fingerprints, Haxe/native compilation, Raylib/Raygui provisioning, runtime content/asset staging, graphical pilot launch, reports, and cache publication. Those responsibilities are useful, but keeping them in one large Python program weakens Caxecraft as an end-to-end Haxe showcase and makes host tooling harder to share with the editor and future packaged game. This is low priority behind playable content and engine correctness.
design: First inventory play.py responsibilities and identify the smallest natural Haxe modules: typed command/config parsing, build request/state, runtime package staging, process execution, pilot launch/reporting, and provisioning adapters. Move one independently verifiable slice at a time, preserving existing commands and no-build content feedback. Use typed c.* or platform externs for host filesystem/process boundaries that haxe.c can express. A tiny bootstrap shell is acceptable only where needed to build or locate the Haxe launcher; do not replace one monolithic script with another wrapper or compile game content into the launcher. Delete Python owners as each Haxe owner reaches parity.
acceptance_criteria: A responsibility map and migration order exist; at least one vertical launcher command runs from Haxe compiled through haxe.c; build/content fingerprints and fail-closed cache behavior retain focused parity; Raylib/Raygui provisioning, native tool invocation, runtime package staging, no-build content feedback, pilot reports, deterministic paths, timeouts, cleanup, and cross-platform claims each have an explicit final owner; reloadable content remains outside compile identity; play.py shrinks monotonically and is deleted when all required commands have verified Haxe ownership; any unavoidable non-Haxe bootstrap is minimal, documented, and separately justified; Caxecraft gameplay/content work is not blocked on this migration.
notes: Requested as low-priority follow-up on 2026-08-10. Do not begin as a big-bang rewrite; content/gameplay remains the near-term priority.

title: Reduce the Caxecraft campaign-runtime native proof below its original budget
description: The multi-NPC/runtime-asset content change made the complete campaign-runtime Eval/native/sanitizer command exceed its 20-second per-native execution timeout twice in isolation. A 40-second containment keeps semantic evidence in place, but the full command measured 87.04 seconds on 2026-08-09. Profile parsing, package reads, generated runtime allocation, and duplicate sanitizer work before changing topology.
acceptance_criteria: Measure phase timings on an unsaturated host; identify the first real native bottleneck; restore a reviewed per-run budget at or below 20 seconds or document a better evidence-backed budget; preserve Eval/native equality, sanitizer coverage, package boundary checks, and all campaign-runtime scenarios.

title: Measure the Caxecraft content-only loop percentile
description:
## Why

The architectural outcome is not merely a faster compiler: content-only edits
must avoid compilation entirely. Without process and timing evidence, a cache
or stale executable can make the loop look fast while running old content.

## What

Measure and enforce the first runtime level/UI content loop on an unsaturated
declared host.

## How

Instrument file read/hash, lex, parse, validate, registry/plan resolution,
candidate construction, publication, and first-ready state. Audit child
processes and fail if Haxe, haxe.c, a C compiler, or a linker starts. Record
exact source hashes, content hit/miss, generation ID, cold/off behavior, CPU,
RSS, host load, median, MAD, and at least five samples. The accepted p95 is at
or below two seconds; a slow correct native path remains correct work to
profile, never justification to restore generated authority.
acceptance_criteria: Map, pack, and UI edits report exact input hashes, content hit/miss and generation identity; process auditing proves no Haxe, haxe.c, C compiler, or linker starts; read/hash, lex, parse, validate, registry/plan resolve, candidate build, publication and first-ready phases are timed with CPU/RSS/host load; at least five uncontended samples record median, MAD and p95 at or below two seconds on a declared host; cold/off and failed-load paths remain authoritative and fail closed.
notes:
2026-08-01 dependency correction: all runtime-loading implementation prerequisites are complete through .7.4 and the frontend budget is restored through .7.5. This issue is now the explicit remaining acceptance owner for aggregate .7's no-build pack/UI edit; .7 waits for this evidence rather than blocking it.
2026-08-01 behavior-first red: scenario owner is the interactive playable build-state boundary. Given a previously verified executable and a valid authored pack/UI edit, requesting play must preserve the executable-build hit, restage and load the edited runtime bytes, and start no Haxe/C/compiler/linker process; malformed content must fail before readiness without publishing a false hit. Independent expected hashes come from Python hashlib over manually selected source files, while the compiled Haxe loader is the real consumer observer. Focused command: python3 test/governance/test_caxecraft_build_state.py CaxecraftBuildStateTests.test_playable_wires_every_semantic_input_family. It failed for the intended reason: repo/caxecraft/locales (and, after that first assertion, packs) remain in play_build_inputs, so runtime-authored data still invalidates the code build.
2026-08-01 incremental implementation: map, pack, and UI authored bytes were removed from the executable build key while generated compatibility Haxe remains a build input for .8. A dedicated memory/software profile now reports exact independent hashlib receipts, cache hit/miss, generation and runtime UI/pack observations, ordered read/hash/lex/parse/validate/resolve/build/publication/first-ready phases, child CPU/RSS, host load, and a bounded one-authorized-child launcher audit. Tool identities are read from executable bytes without starting version processes. A valid-JSON/wrong-type UI case proves the compiled loader rejects after registry resolution and before publication/readiness; the launcher exits nonzero and retains its report. Focused governance is 5/5 and build-state is 16/16; the real runtime-content-generation Eval/native/sanitizer tracer passes. Distinct review found and fixed a partial-line timeout escape by replacing blocking line iteration with selector-driven nonblocking byte reads; it also bounded the process claim to the launcher path and admitted generated profile. The first five map samples [2109.804, 1573.980, 1539.917, 1513.290, 1479.653] had median 1539.917ms, MAD 34.063ms, observed p95 2002.639ms and were correctly rejected 2.639ms over budget. Subsequent host load reached 38 on 12 CPUs; the final low-contention map/pack/UI portfolio remains pending and no saturated result advances the claim.
2026-08-01 host-blocked portfolio retries: one run reached five representative map samples (1831.307, 1529.608, 1472.689, 1508.129, 1451.831ms) and four representative pack samples (1458.505, 1484.144, 1472.784, 1667.296ms); a fifth pack attempt was rejected as contended, then unrelated host load rose as high as 36.725 and stayed above the 4.8 launch threshold for 120 checks. The profiler was hardened to atomically checkpoint collecting, failed-budget, insufficient-sample, and interrupted-host evidence. A final 240-check/20-minute attempt never saw load below 4.8, admitted zero timing samples, and wrote status interrupted-host for Darwin 24.4.0 arm64 with 12 logical CPUs; setup performed no build and the malformed-load runtimeOutcome was rejected. No threshold was weakened and no busy sample was counted. The issue remains in progress solely for one quiet-host complete map/pack/UI portfolio.
2026-08-02 paused at maintainer request while haxe_c-xge.37 consolidates excessive Caxecraft Python entry points. All .9 work remains isolated in the current worktree; the performance portfolio is still the only unmet .9 acceptance item.
2026-08-02 resumed-profile red/fix: the public profile launched its setup at one-minute load 5.75/12 and the unchanged 20s launcher containment timeout fired before any evidence was collected. This exposed drift between the original 40% pre-launch headroom and the 50% representative-sample ceiling. Focused red command: python3 test/governance/test_caxecraft_content_loop.py CaxecraftContentLoopTests.test_sample_launch_keeps_headroom_below_the_acceptance_ceiling; mocked load 5.0/12 returned ready=True. host_ready now again requires <=40% before spending a sample, while play.py still admits a representative sample only when both start/end load are <=50%; the evidence definition was not weakened. The focused test is green, all 7 content-loop governance tests pass, all 16 build-state tests pass, and the timed-out run preserved the existing checkpoint.
2026-08-02 maintainer reprioritization: runtime map/pack/UI files should be ordinary runtime data, so formal five-sample <=2s percentile collection must not block game/compiler progress. The large Python portfolio observer, Haxe phase-print protocol, npm profile command, percentile documentation, and profile-only tests were removed before commit. Retained correctness/scalability contract: authored map/pack/UI paths are absent from the executable build key; each launch stages and SHA-256-receipts exact current bytes; reuse identity hashes tool executables without starting compiler/version processes; the compiled Haxe runtime-content tracer reads, validates, resolves, and publishes the real bundle through Eval, strict native C, ASan, and UBSan; malformed paths remain fail closed. Focused build-state is 15/15 and full governance is 224/224. The <=2s p95 acceptance remains explicitly unproven and this issue stays open at P3; it no longer blocks runtime-authority removal or aggregate gameplay progress.
2026-08-09 residual content-loop finding from haxe_c-xge.20.2.3: `npm run caxecraft:content:validate` refused reuse with `build input changed: repo/caxecraft/play.hxml` even immediately after the ordinary memory-software launch-smoke pilot rebuilt and passed. The real Adventure journey separately proved current-content restaging against an unchanged executable in 320.5 ms, so this selector mismatch does not invalidate objective-state semantics and does not advance the deferred percentile claim. Diagnose the launch-smoke request/reuse identity before using the short validator as evidence.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
2026-08-02 scalability observation from the completed compact village: expanding the canonical level to 1,031 terrain runs made the complete unoptimized runtime-level-loader native parser/publication fault matrix exceed its prior 20-second per-process containment on this host. The same lane passes with a bounded 40-second diagnostic timeout, while the focused landmark, aquatics, inventory, session, package, adventure-journey, and real native pilot proofs remain green.

This is not evidence for a gameplay load-time regression or for the <=2s p95 claim: the affected command deliberately performs a broad malformed-input and sanitizer matrix rather than one representative launch. No performance threshold was weakened and no speed claim is being advanced. The formal cold/warm uncontended map/pack/UI percentile portfolio remains deferred here as the maintainer requested; this note preserves the richer-content maintenance signal for later profiling.

title: Research lifetime-safe retained C views in Haxe classes
description: Caxecraft exposed a misleading pressure to store a borrowed WorldCells/Span inside WaterSimulation. The natural game design does not need that retained alias: WaterSimulation owns its private queue and borrows the shared world for each operation. However, metal-facing Haxe APIs may eventually need an object to retain a view whose owner has a provably longer lifetime. Today span fields correctly fail closed because Haxe source has no general lifetime syntax and haxe.c must not emit a dangling C pointer. Research the smallest sound model rather than weakening the stored-span negative. Compare parent-owned embedded objects, constructor-scoped borrows, explicit owner tokens/regions, nonescaping whole-program proofs, copying/ownership alternatives, and diagnostics. This is future capability work, not a blocker for Caxecraft.
acceptance_criteria: Document concrete motivating source shapes and rejected unsafe cases; identify whether a sound retained-view model can be expressed through existing Haxe types/metadata and whole-program facts without a general borrow checker; specify HxcIR/analysis/runtime/ABI effects and one-owner legality; retain fail-closed stored-span behavior until positive and negative lifetime proofs exist; if implementation is recommended, define focused Eval/native C, sanitizer, generated-C, escape-negative, and Caxecraft-independent acceptance gates.

title: Audit optimal Haxe compilation-server reuse for haxe.c
description: Compare haxe.c's current cold/prime/warm server lifecycle and HXML resolution with ../haxe.elixir.codex and ../hxhx (Reflaxe.OCaml), then check the pinned server implementation and invalidation behavior in ../haxe.compilerdev.reference/haxe. Determine whether the existing isolated server harness is optimal and whether caxecraft:play or the future hxc dev loop should enable it by default. Keep this as tooling R&D; do not cache TypedExpr, CompilationContext, output ownership, or other request-mutable compiler state.
acceptance_criteria: Map haxe.c, Reflaxe.Elixir, and hxhx/Reflaxe.OCaml server ownership, port selection, HXML/library resolution, invalidation, shutdown, diagnostics, and watcher integration with file/line evidence; inspect the pinned Haxe server source for the exact reuse/reset boundary; preserve reproducible cold, prime, and warm Haxe-to-generated-C measurements and explicitly separate native compilation/linking; inventory existing haxe.c byte-parity and request-leakage evidence; publish an adopt/adjust/reject recommendation with server modes, compatibility identity, lifecycle, retry, cache boundary, and required implementation tests; feed the accepted behavior into haxe_c-5sd.8.2 without weakening cold CI proofs. One-Haxe-edit native timing and dependency invalidation belong to haxe_c-5sd.8.3 after depfile/object reuse makes that measurement truthful.
notes: 2026-07-27 audit result: adopt an owned Haxe server as a bounded frontend accelerator for changed-source development, after an exact unchanged-build hit and before fresh request-local haxe.c lowering. The audit is published in docs/research/haxe-server-audit.md. It checks the pinned Haxe 5 reset/cache implementation and compares the lifecycle designs in Reflaxe.Elixir and hxhx/Reflaxe.OCaml. The original R&D acceptance mixed design research with crash/lifecycle implementation and a one-module native benchmark that cannot be truthful before incremental object reuse exists. Those executable gates remain on haxe_c-5sd.8.2 and haxe_c-5sd.8.3 rather than being weakened or simulated here.
close_reason: Published the pinned-Haxe and sibling-server audit, adopted a bounded owned-server contract, preserved existing cold/prime/warm evidence, and assigned crash-safe lifecycle plus native edit timing to their truthful implementation owners.

title: Measure an Eval-assisted playable development loop
description: Explore whether Caxecraft can offer a faster playable iteration loop while keeping shared game code on Haxe Eval and delegating native presentation/services through a narrow helper or adapter. This is an R&D experiment, not a claim that the game currently runs on Eval.
design: Compare a haxe.c-built native Raylib helper over bounded stdin/stdout IPC, an admitted Eval native-extension boundary if available in the pinned toolchain, a lightweight Eval presentation adapter, and the existing incremental haxe.c plus incremental C build. Also compare a JavaScript/Web adapter as more useful cross-target product evidence. Keep the direct C path authoritative; do not introduce a frame-by-frame serialization architecture without measured benefit.
acceptance_criteria: A small executable spike records cold/warm edit-to-frame latency, per-frame/control overhead, shared-code percentage, process/resource lifecycle, debugging experience, failure modes, and implementation/maintenance cost for each viable option. The recommendation either demonstrates a materially faster sound loop or rejects the helper approach with evidence; docs continue to say only the domain runs on Eval until a playable probe exists.
notes: If the spike demonstrates a real benefit, shape the result as an optional reusable haxe.c development component rather than Caxecraft-only glue: a documented native host/reload or helper boundary that can run target-neutral Haxe logic quickly before a full native rebuild. Keep it out of release artifacts and runtime plans unless explicitly selected. Final correctness, generated-C quality, ABI, sanitizers, and packaging still require the authoritative complete haxe.c/native build. Define which code can reload, compatibility/version checks, state reset/migration, resource ownership, failure recovery, and a clean fallback when the helper is absent.

title: Explore conditional-light cross-target adapter architecture for Caxecraft and RaylibHx
description: Caxecraft's portable rules should not accumulate scattered #if branches as JavaScript, Rust, Go, WebAssembly, or other rendering/input ports are explored. Define a practical architecture in which shared game state, semantic input, scenarios, localization, saves, and tests use target-neutral Haxe types while each target supplies its own rendering, input, audio, persistence, and resource adapter. Prefer target-specific classpaths/source sets or one composition root so ordinary modules do not need target conditionals. Carefully retain #if only where it truthfully gates a C-only ABI package, compile-time test seam, or representation whose safe meaning does not exist on another target.
design: Compare three bounded options with small executable probes: (1) target-specific source roots containing the same adapter module names, (2) shared structural interfaces with target-owned implementations selected at one composition root, and (3) narrow conditional typedef/import aliases. Evaluate Haxe DCE, custom-target activation, package distribution, IDE completion, diagnostics, generated C quality, allocation/dynamic-dispatch cost, ownership cleanup, and compatibility with sibling Reflaxe compilers. Do not invent a universal graphics engine or universal IR. The result should state where conditionals are allowed, show a before/after Caxecraft module layout, and recommend a migration that preserves the direct Raylib/C path.
acceptance_criteria: An ADR or architecture note defines the portable core and per-target adapter boundaries; at least C and one non-C probe compile from the same shared gameplay source; target choice is localized to a documented composition/source-set boundary; ordinary domain/scenario/localization modules contain no target conditionals or foreign API types; C-only Raylib ABI declarations remain fail-closed rather than pretending portability; generated C retains direct calls, explicit ownership, no unexpected runtime/dynamic dispatch/allocation, and readable structure; the note distinguishes justified compile-time conditionals from avoidable scattered branches and gives incremental migration/test gates.
notes:
2026-07-21 application pressure confirms the intended rule: actor state, AI, interaction, inventory gifts, authored meadow geometry, and pilot intent remain ordinary target-neutral Haxe with no target conditionals. Main contains one compile-time scripted-input provider choice because release builds must exclude the pilot channel. Future work should prefer target-specific source roots or one composition root before adding further conditionals.
The first combat increment follows this rule: PlayerVitals, Mossling combat, BerryDrop, Inventory, and pilot intent are shared ordinary Haxe with no target conditional or raylib type. Compile-time choices remain at the C raylib application/provider boundary. This is the practical pattern to preserve while haxe_c-xge.34 evaluates whether target-specific source roots can make even that boundary clearer.
RecoveryUse demonstrates the careful-conditional rule: the damaged initial fixture is selected only at the compile-time pilot composition boundary, while Recovery, PlayerVitals, inventory consumption, and primary/secondary intent remain ordinary target-neutral Haxe. No target conditional was added to gameplay. A future source-set design may move the provider selection out of Main, but it must keep release builds free of pilot state and retain direct raylib calls.

title: Explore Rust and JavaScript adapters for the Caxecraft domain after the C showcase
description:
Follow up only after the native C/raylib showcase is playable and evidence-backed. Reuse the renderer-independent domain seam to test whether the same game logic can compile through future Rust and JavaScript targets while each target keeps an idiomatic platform/rendering adapter.

This issue is intentionally outside the RaylibHx/Caxecraft delivery epic so it cannot delay or distort the C-first design. Evaluate the real cost of replacing fixed c.CArray storage, c.Float32 boundary conversions, and raylib input/rendering with portable or target-specific carriers. Use shared deterministic traces to separate domain portability from rendering/backend differences.

Non-scope: imposing lowest-common-denominator APIs on the first C version, promising source compatibility before experiments, or treating raylib as a Rust/JavaScript abstraction.
acceptance_criteria:
- The accepted C domain boundary and deterministic trace suite are inventoried before any porting change.
- Rust and JavaScript prototypes isolate storage, clock/input, rendering, and native-resource adapters while keeping gameplay algorithms shared where semantics truly match.
- Cross-target state traces report integer, floating-point, iteration, and collision differences explicitly.
- Performance, code size, runtime, ownership, and ergonomics tradeoffs are measured per target.
- Any common abstraction is introduced only after two working adapters prove it, with no regression to the direct C/raylib path.

title: [HXC-E9-T12] Prove a WebAssembly/TypeScript bridge
description:
Stable plan key: E9.T12
Requirement IDs: HXC-PROD-010, HXC-EX-008, HXC-DOC-008
PRD sections: §7.4, §19.1

Context: Compile a small exported C ABI module through WASI or Emscripten and consume it from TypeScript with explicit memory/ownership wrappers.

Scope: Compile a small exported C ABI module through WASI or Emscripten and consume it from TypeScript with explicit memory/ownership wrappers.

Non-scope: Work outside this outcome and its acceptance criteria. Create a linked discovered-from issue instead of silently widening scope.

Dependencies: E7.T10, E8.T04, E5.T04

Validation: Satisfy every acceptance item with executable evidence and the applicable PRD §40 definition-of-done gates; record exact commands and artifacts in the close reason.

Compatibility: Assess and document portable/metal, runtime-policy, environment, generated-C, and public-ABI impact where applicable. Do not harden an unresolved public contract without an accepted ADR.

Documentation: Update affected ADRs, documentation, diagnostics, capability data, and ledgers required by the acceptance criteria and PRD §40.
acceptance_criteria:
- Build is reproducible and uses the same export ABI model.
- String/buffer transfer and errors are demonstrated.
- Generated JS/TS glue is scoped and documented.
- Example makes no claim of general TypeScript compatibility.

title: Evaluate native OCaml promotion for the haxe.c target core
description: After reproducible phase profiling and after the haxe.ocaml M22 shared-host SDK is executable rather than planning-only, evaluate compiling haxe.c target logic from the same Haxe sources into a native OCaml Reflaxe plugin or builtin. The goal is lower compiler latency without a semantic fork or loss of the direct stock-Haxe recovery path.
design: Keep the stock-Haxe/Reflaxe activation and TypedExpr capture as a thin host adapter. Make the target core request-local and host-neutral where evidence justifies it: frozen typed facts/HxcIR, validators, optimization and representation plans, naming, declaration/layout planning, CAST, printing, manifests, and transactional artifact planning remain one Haxe implementation. Follow ../haxe.ocaml M22: one semantic target core, preferably one promoted payload, with only typed/versioned host adapters and negotiated services. Do not introduce a second C backend, a universal IR, per-expression RPC, or speculative abstraction solely for this future lane. Profile first; native promotion is accepted only if it improves a named dominant cost after ordinary algorithmic, caching, reporting, and process-reuse work.
acceptance_criteria: A source inventory separates macro/compiler-object dependencies from promotable target-core code and names the smallest adapter boundary; the exact haxe.ocaml/hxhx SDK version and capability contract are pinned; the same frozen program produces byte-identical normal C/build/ABI artifacts and equivalent structured diagnostics through evaluated and native routes; cold, warm, no-op, one-module edit, peak-RSS, and backend-only benchmarks show a reviewed material improvement and attribute remaining Haxe typing cost; compiler-server/reentrancy, cancellation, malformed transport, ABI mismatch, plugin load/unload, and fallback tests pass; direct pinned Haxe/HXML compilation remains documented and functional; no readiness claim is made while the shared stock-Haxe/hxhx plugin ABI remains planning-only.
notes:
This records the project-owner hypothesis from 2026-07-19. ../haxe.ocaml/docs/00-project/REFLAXE_NATIVE_COMPILER_SDK_M22_PLAN.md explicitly aims for normal Haxe + portable Reflaxe, one target implementation, native OCaml promotion, and the same payload in stock Haxe or hxhx. Expected reuse is nearly all semantic target logic, not literally all host glue. It may accelerate backend execution; it cannot by itself remove Haxe parse/type time.
The intended high-upside experiment is the combined route, not only a native backend under stock Haxe: a native hxhx parse/type/macro host feeding the same haxe.c core compiled by reflaxe.ocaml as a plugin or builtin could remove Eval from both major compiler-side execution layers. Current hard prerequisites include parity for this repositorys pinned Haxe 5.0.0-preview.1 TypedExpr/macro/custom-target surface (hxhx currently declares Haxe 4.3.7 compatibility as its active goal) and a shipped M22 shared host SDK. Compare end-to-end and phase-isolated timings; do not infer speed from native packaging alone.
Project-owner clarification: this is deliberately optional and may never be pursued. It must not block the normal Haxe/Reflaxe compiler, Caxecraft, release milestones, or near-term performance work. Revisit only if profiling shows remaining compiler-host overhead worth the added SDK/plugin complexity.
